claims.claim: In a UK cluster RCT of 4340 people aged 75+, universal vision screening did not improve vision 3-5 years later compared with targeted screening.
claims.supporting_passage: Three to five years after screening, the relative risk of having visual acuity < 6/18 in either eye, comparing universal with targeted screening, was 1.07 (95% confidence interval 0.84 to 1.36; P = 0.58). The mean composite score of the visual function questionnaire was 85.6 in the targeted screening group and 86.0 in the universal group (difference 0.4, 95% confidence interval -1.7 to 2.5, P = 0.69). ... Including a vision screening component by a practice nurse in a pragmatic trial of multidimensional screening for older people did not lead to improved visual outcomes.
claims.pico_timeframe: People 75+ in 20 UK practices / universal nurse-led acuity screening + referral / targeted screening (only those with health problems assessed) / acuity <6/18 either eye, VFQ-25 / 3-5 years
claims.safe_wording: In a UK trial of 4340 people aged 75 and over, testing everyone's eyesight as part of a health check did not leave people seeing better three to five years later than a check that tested only some people.
claims.qualifications: Comparator was targeted screening, not no screening. Non-significant result: 'did not show a clear difference'.

numbers.meaning: relative risk of acuity <6/18 either eye, universal vs targeted, 3-5 y
VFQ-25 mean scores, universal vs targeted

claims.claim: A Cochrane review found vision screening of older people in the community did not improve vision; most likely reason was low take-up of offered intervention.
claims.supporting_passage: The evidence from RCTs undertaken to date does not support vision screening for older people living independently in a community setting, whether in isolation or as part of a multi-component screening package. ... The most likely reason for this negative review is that the populations within the trials often did not take up the offered intervention as a result of the vision screening and large proportions of those who did not have vision screening appeared to seek their own intervention.
claims.pico_timeframe: People 65+ living independently / community vision screening / no screening or standard care / vision outcomes / 1-5 years; 10 RCTs, 10,608 people
claims.safe_wording: A Cochrane review of 10 trials in over 10,000 older people found community vision screening did not improve eyesight. The reviewers thought the most likely reason was that people often did not take up the treatment offered after screening, while many unscreened people sought help themselves.
claims.qualifications: Reasons are the reviewers' interpretation, not a tested finding. Applies to people living independently; the reviewers suggest testing more dependent people.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Does not show that correcting sight is ineffective; it shows screening alone did not change outcomes.

numbers.meaning: risk of 'not seeing well', screened vs not, 6 studies, 4522 people

claims.claim: After first-eye cataract surgery, a substantial share of people may be left with a large difference between the eyes (symptomatic anisometropia) until the second eye is done.
claims.supporting_passage: 57% of patients were awaiting first eye surgery, and 32% of those patients would be at risk of symptomatic anisometropia postoperatively. [Ishikawa:] We found "moderate" evidence supporting improvement in stereopsis, stereoacuity, and anisometropia over and above the benefits of first-eye surgery.
claims.pico_timeframe: Belfast waiting-list cohort 2020 (estimated risk); systematic review of second-eye surgery
claims.safe_wording: After the first cataract operation, the two eyes can end up needing very different glasses. In one Belfast waiting list, about 1 in 3 people waiting for their first eye were judged at risk of this troublesome imbalance. Second-eye surgery helps even it out.
claims.qualifications: The 32% is an estimated risk in one clinic sample, not measured symptoms. No source opened for the specific advice to remove or change the lens on the operated side; present it only as a question to ask the optician or eye team.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Guidance leaflet (NHS/RCOphth) not opened; NICE NG77 not opened.

numbers.meaning: of 179 awaiting first-eye surgery, estimated at risk of symptomatic anisometropia, Belfast 2020

claims.claim: In an RCT of 239 women over 70, expedited second-eye surgery improved visual function and confidence; the reduction in falls was not statistically significant.
claims.supporting_passage: visual function (especially stereopsis) improved in the operated group. ... Rate of falling was reduced by 32% in the operated group, but this was not statistically significant (rate ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.39, 1.19, P = 0.18). Confidence, visual disability and handicap all improved in the operated compared with the control group. ... The effect on rate of falling remains uncertain.
claims.pico_timeframe: 239 women >70 with one unoperated cataract / surgery ~4 weeks / routine ~12 month wait / falls diary 12 months, health status 6 months
claims.safe_wording: In a trial of 239 women over 70, having the second eye done within about a month rather than waiting a year improved their sight and confidence. Whether it reduced falls was uncertain.
claims.qualifications: Women only; do not quote 32% as a benefit.

claims.claim: NICE NG77 recommends access to cataract surgery is not restricted on visual acuity and that referral considers impact on daily life.
claims.safe_wording: Not usable: NICE NG77 could not be opened (web blocked; not in Drive).

claims.claim: In an RCT of 306 women over 70, expedited first-eye cataract surgery reduced the rate of falling by 34% and fewer had fractures.
claims.supporting_passage: 306 women aged over 70, with cataract, were randomised to expedited (approximately 4 weeks) or routine (12 months wait) surgery. ... Rate of falling was reduced by 34% in the operated group (rate ratio 0.66, 95% confidence interval 0.45 to 0.96, p = 0.03). ... Four participants in the operated group had fractures (3%), compared with 12 (8%) in the control group (p = 0.04).
claims.pico_timeframe: 306 women >70 / first-eye surgery ~4 weeks / ~12 months wait / falls 12 months
claims.safe_wording: In a trial of 306 women over 70, those who had their first cataract removed within about a month had about a third fewer falls over the next year than women who waited about a year; 3 in 100 had a fracture compared with 8 in 100.
claims.qualifications: Women only; proportion who fell at least once was not lower (49% vs 45%); the reduction was in rate of falls.

claims.claim: Charles Bonnet syndrome: complex visual hallucinations in people with sight loss who keep insight; linked to acquired visual loss, often AMD.
claims.supporting_passage: Charles Bonnet syndrome (CBS) is characterised by recurrent, complex and vivid visual hallucinations in the absence of cognitive dysfunction. Individuals with CBS usually maintain insight into the unreal nature of their hallucinatory experiences. There is a strong association between CBS and acquired visual loss and the most commonly described ocular pathology is age-related macular degeneration.
claims.safe_wording: Some people with sight loss, most often from macular degeneration, see vivid images that are not there, and know they are not real. This is called Charles Bonnet syndrome.

claims.claim: Teunisse 1996: 60 of 505 met criteria; all had full insight; correct diagnosis in 1 of 16 who saw a doctor; all glad to be told not mental illness.
claims.supporting_passage: After screening 505 visually handicapped patients, 60 were found to meet proposed diagnostic criteria for CBS ... all patients had full insight into the unreal nature of their hallucinations. ... CBS caused considerable distress in only 17 (28%) patients. However, all patients were glad to be told that their hallucinations were not due to mental disease. The proper diagnosis had been made in only one of the 16 patients who had consulted a doctor.
claims.pico_timeframe: 505 visually impaired patients, Dutch clinic population, 1990s, cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a Dutch study of 505 people attending with sight loss, 60 had these images. All knew the images were not real. Of 16 who had seen a doctor about them, only 1 had been given the right explanation. All were glad to hear it was not mental illness.
claims.qualifications: Clinic population from 1996; do not generalise 60/505 to all people with sight loss.

numbers.meaning: correctly diagnosed among those who consulted a doctor

claims.claim: CBS is a diagnosis of exclusion; new hallucinations need assessment for other causes; information about benign nature is key treatment.
claims.supporting_passage: It is widely agreed that CBS is an underreported diagnosis caused by patients' reluctance to admit their hallucinatory experience because of fear of being labelled mentally ill. CBS is a diagnosis of exclusion and careful assessment must be made to ensure that other etiologies causing the symptoms are ruled out. ... Thus, a major part of the treatment is careful information about the benign nature of the condition.
claims.safe_wording: People often keep these images to themselves for fear of being thought mentally ill. New hallucinations should still be mentioned to a doctor, because other causes need to be ruled out. Explaining the condition is a large part of the help.
claims.qualifications: Source does not list delirium, Lewy body dementia etc. specifically; keep to 'other causes' or source separately. Advice that eye clinics mention CBS at diagnosis is judgement, mark as 'we should'.

claims.claim: Timolol eye drops enter the circulation and cause systemic beta-blockade; case reports describe complete heart block resolving on stopping.
claims.supporting_passage: Despite its topical administration, ophthalmic timolol enters systemic circulation and produces a systemic beta-adrenergic blockade. ... Electrocardiography indicated a heart rate (HR) of 29 bpm with complete atrioventricular (AV) block ... The AV block and bradycardia resolved 48-h after timolol cessation.
claims.pico_timeframe: Single case, 62-year-old man, 13 years of timolol
claims.safe_wording: Timolol eye drops get into the bloodstream and can act like a beta-blocker tablet. Case reports describe very slow heart rates and heart block that settled when the drops were stopped.
claims.qualifications: Case reports show it can happen, not how often. In this case an underlying conduction problem was unmasked.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: BNF/SPC cautions not opened; do not state contraindications list or press duration from BNF.

numbers.meaning: time to resolution after stopping, single case

claims.claim: Nasolacrimal occlusion (5 min) and tissue press method both lowered plasma timolol vs no intervention.
claims.supporting_passage: These were: (a) nasolacrimal (punctal) occlusion for 5 min, (b) tissue press method or (c) no intervention. Timolol plasma levels were measured 1 h after drop application. ... Plasma timolol concentrations after tissue press method and NLO were significantly lower than those without intervention.
claims.pico_timeframe: 21 adults / NLO 5 min or tissue press / none / plasma timolol at 1 h
claims.safe_wording: In a small cross-over study, pressing on the inner corner of the eye for 5 minutes after the drop, or a tissue press, lowered the amount of timolol reaching the blood.
claims.qualifications: 21 adults, not older patients; surrogate outcome; clinical benefit not shown. Use '5 minutes' only as the trial's method.

numbers.meaning: duration of nasolacrimal occlusion in trial

candidates.reason: Smeeth 2003 and Cochrane 2018 support the null result and the take-up explanation (as reviewers' interpretation). Evans 2004 causes claim not needed.
Anisometropia risk and Foss 2006 supported; no NHS/RCOphth leaflet or NICE NG77 opened for glasses-lens advice or second-eye criteria.
candidates.revised_angle: After the first eye, the two eyes can need very different glasses (about 1 in 3 at risk in one Belfast list); second-eye surgery evens this out and improved sight and confidence in a trial of women over 70, falls effect uncertain. Close with the question to ask before surgery: 'What should I do about my glasses until the second eye is done?' Do not state specific lens advice or NICE criteria.

candidates.reason: Core claim (NICE NG77 on acuity thresholds and referral by impact) could not be opened; complication rate (NOD audit) not found. Harwood 2005 alone does not carry the angle.
Teunisse figures confirmed (60/505, 1 of 16, all full insight, all glad); diagnosis-of-exclusion point supported by review.
Systemic absorption, case reports and occlusion trial supported; BNF cautions and press duration from BNF not opened.
candidates.revised_angle: Keep teaching point with case-report framing ('can happen', not frequency); give 5 minutes as the trial method only; say absorption-reduction lowered blood levels but clinical benefit is unproven; omit BNF contraindication list; alternatives in general terms ('other types of glaucoma drops exist; discuss with the eye team').
